body.statement:
For every \(2\leq k\leq m\) and \(r\geq1\),
\[
mr\leq s_\star(m,r,k)\leq2mr-m.
\]
Consequently \(s_\star(m,r,k)=\Theta(mr)\) with constants uniform in \(k\).  The upper bound controls both separately minimized endpoint supports \(s_L(o,e)\) and \(s_U(o,e)\) for every \((o,e)\in\mathcal C_{m,r,k}\).  The lower bound is witnessed by the compatible family \(o_{is}=1/(mr)\), \(e_{js}=1/r\) for every \(i,j\in\mathcal X\) and \(s\in\mathcal Y\), for which both endpoint support minima are at least \(mr\).  Hence the quadratic \(k^2\) term in \(N_\star\) is removable uniformly for exact endpoint support, although these bounds do not determine the optimal finite constant between the displayed lower and upper values.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(2\leq k\leq m\) and \(r\geq1\).  Let \((o,e)\in\mathcal C_{m,r,k}\).  By the sharp-interval theorem, there are laws \(Q_L,Q_U\in\mathcal Q(o,e)\) satisfying
\[
Q_L\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in\mathcal J}A_j\right)=L(o,e),
\qquad
Q_U\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in\mathcal J}A_j\right)=U(o,e).
\]
Apply the certificate-preserving support-compression lemma separately to \(Q_L\) and \(Q_U\).  The resulting endpoint laws have support at most
\[
mr+m(r-1)=2mr-m.
\]
By the definitions of the two separate endpoint support minima,
\[
s_L(o,e)\leq2mr-m,
\qquad
s_U(o,e)\leq2mr-m.
\]
Taking their maximum and then the supremum over \(\mathcal C_{m,r,k}\) gives
\[
s_\star(m,r,k)\leq2mr-m.
\]

For the reverse inequality, define margins by
\[
o_{is}=\frac1{mr}
\quad(i\in\mathcal X,\ s\in\mathcal Y),
\qquad
e_{js}=\frac1r
\quad(j\in\mathcal X,\ s\in\mathcal Y).
\]
The observational entries are nonnegative and sum to
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal X}\sum_{s\in\mathcal Y}o_{is}
=mr\frac1{mr}=1.
\]
Every intervention row is nonnegative and satisfies
\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal Y}e_{js}=r\frac1r=1.
\]
Moreover, \(k\leq m\) and \(k\geq2\) imply \(m\geq1\), whence
\[
e_{is}=\frac1r\geq\frac1{mr}=o_{is}
\]
for every \(i\in\mathcal X\) and \(s\in\mathcal Y\).  The compatibility theorem therefore implies \((o,e)\in\mathcal C_{m,r,k}\).

Let \(Q\in\mathcal Q(o,e)\) be arbitrary.  For \(i\in\mathcal X\) and \(s\in\mathcal Y\), define the observational response cell
\[
C_{is}=\{(x,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y^m:x=i,\ y_i=s\}.
\]
The \(mr\) cells \(C_{is}\) are pairwise disjoint: two atoms in cells with different \(i\) have different factual-treatment labels, while for fixed \(i\) the coordinate \(y_i\) cannot equal two different labels.  They exhaust \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y^m\).  By the observational-margin restriction in the definition of \(\mathcal Q(o,e)\),
\[
Q(C_{is})=o_{is}=\frac1{mr}>0.
\]
The response space is finite.  Therefore every positive-mass cell contains at least one positive-mass atom of \(Q\).  Because the cells are disjoint, these atoms are distinct, and hence
\[
\sigma(Q)\geq mr.
\]
The sharp-interval theorem ensures that both endpoint faces are nonempty.  The preceding inequality applies to every law on either face, so minimization over those faces gives
\[
s_L(o,e)\geq mr,
\qquad
s_U(o,e)\geq mr.
\]
This single compatible margin pair therefore yields
\[
s_\star(m,r,k)
=\sup_{(o',e')\in\mathcal C_{m,r,k}}
\max\{s_L(o',e'),s_U(o',e')\}
\geq mr.
\]
Combining the two directions,
\[
mr\leq s_\star(m,r,k)\leq2mr-m\leq2mr.
\]
The comparison constants \(1\) and \(2\) do not depend on \(k\), proving \(s_\star(m,r,k)=\Theta(mr)\) uniformly in \(k\).  Finally,
\[
N_\star=m+2m(r-1)+k^2+3k+1
=(2mr-m)+k^2+3k+1,
\]
whereas both exact endpoint witnesses always admit support at most \(2mr-m\).  Thus the quadratic \(k^2\) term is an overhead of the explicit grid-preserving construction, not an intrinsic requirement for exact endpoint support.  The argument supplies matching asymptotic order but does not assert that either finite constant \(1\) or \(2-1/r\) is optimal.
